patient.name: Eileen Fitzgerald
patient.setting: Emergency Department, then elderly care ward
patient.complaint: Suddenly confused and seeing things since yesterday
background: Lives alone in Lewisham; independent, does the crossword daily
Started over-the-counter chlorphenamine for itch 4 days ago

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with acute fluctuating confusion in an older patient, or 'most likely cause' (UTI, opiate constipation, anticholinergic drug), with dementias and delirium tremens as distractors.

points: Eileen, 84, brought in by her daughter.
**Suddenly muddled since yesterday**; was doing crosswords last week.
Seeing 'children in the room' at night; pulling at her nightie.
Lucid for an hour this morning, then confused again.

steps.lead: Eileen changed over **a day**, not months, and cannot hold her attention: this is delirium, so search for the cause now.

steps.q: Which feature most strongly suggests delirium rather than dementia in Eileen?
steps.r: Dementia develops over **months** with preserved attention early. Delirium is **acute and fluctuating** with inattention.

steps.lead: Eileen's confusion **fluctuates** and is worse at night; her hallucinations and lower abdominal discomfort fit a UTI trigger.

points: Night: shouting, trying to climb out of bed.
Next morning: **drowsy and quiet**, hard to keep awake.

steps.q: Agitated at night, drowsy and withdrawn by day. Which subtype is this?
steps.r: Alternating hyperactive and hypoactive features is **mixed** delirium.

steps.lead: Eileen swings between both. Her quiet daytime phase is the **hypoactive** form, the easiest to miss.
Eileen has three triggers: a probable **UTI**, regular **codeine** and over-the-counter **chlorphenamine** for itch.

visual.title: Where Eileen is uncomfortable
visual.caption: Lower abdominal discomfort: think UTI, urinary retention and constipation.

steps.text: In confused older patients, check the bladder and bowel.

steps.lead: Delirium raises Eileen's risk of **falls**, a longer stay and death, so it is treated as an emergency.

steps.text: **Hypoactive** delirium looks like tiredness or depression. Screen every drowsy older inpatient.

investigation.exam: Expect the 4AT (score 4 or more) and how to find the cause: urine culture, bloods, CXR, medication review and DRE.

steps.q: Which bedside tool should the nurse use to screen Eileen?
steps.r: The **4AT** is the standard quick delirium screen; MMSE assesses dementia over a longer test.

steps.lead: Eileen's **4AT** takes two minutes and works even if she has an underlying cognitive impairment.

visual.title: Eileen's 4AT score
visual.label: Eileen 8
visual.caption: A score of 4 or above suggests possible delirium.

steps.lead: No scan or blood test makes the diagnosis: Eileen's delirium is **clinical**. Tests find the cause.
Eileen gets the full search: infection screen, medication review, bloods, chest X-ray and a **DRE** because she is on codeine.

steps.title: Eileen's results
steps.text: Infection markers up, mildly dry, E. coli in the urine: a **UTI** trigger.
Do not rely on a dipstick in someone over 65. Send an **MSU** for culture.

management.exam: Expect the stepwise ladder: one-to-one and reorientation, verbal de-escalation, haloperidol, and lorazepam in Parkinson's or Lewy body dementia.

steps.lead: Eileen gets **one-to-one** care, a clock and calendar, her glasses, good lighting, fluids and her daughter at the bedside.

steps.title: Non-drug care first
steps.caption: These measures are first-line for every patient with delirium.

points: Night 2: Eileen **hits a nurse** and pulls out her cannula.
She is trying to climb over the bed rails.
No Parkinson's disease; no Lewy body dementia.

steps.q: Eileen is a risk to herself and staff. What first?
steps.r: **Verbal de-escalation** first: calm, non-confrontational talk, reassurance and reorienting.

steps.q: De-escalation fails and she still risks a fall. She has no Parkinson's or Lewy body dementia. Next?
steps.r: Without Parkinson's or Lewy body dementia, **low-dose haloperidol**, oral before IM.

steps.lead: Eileen can have **haloperidol**. If she had Parkinson's or Lewy body dementia, she would need **lorazepam** instead.
Eileen's real treatment is fixing the triggers: **antibiotics**, a catheter, laxatives, IV fluids and stopping codeine and chlorphenamine.
Eileen's care follows the **4AT** screen and **NICE** delirium guidance: prevent, screen, find the cause, non-drug care first.

visual.title: Eileen's 4AT through admission
visual.caption: As the UTI, retention and constipation are treated, the delirium settles over days.

steps.text: Sedation is a last resort. Treat the **cause**; delirium improves when the trigger is removed.

science.exam: Expect applied mechanisms: cholinergic deficiency with dopamine excess, cytokines across the blood-brain barrier.

steps.lead: Eileen's brain is not structurally damaged: a **systemic insult** (infection, drugs) is disturbing it diffusely.
Relative **cholinergic deficiency** with dopamine excess explains why chlorphenamine tipped Eileen over and why haloperidol settles her.

steps.q: Why did Eileen's chlorphenamine make her worse?
steps.r: **Anticholinergics** deepen the cholinergic deficit; they also cause dry mouth and **urinary retention**.

steps.lead: Eileen's UTI released **cytokines** that crossed the blood-brain barrier and disrupted neuronal function.
At 84 Eileen has little **cognitive reserve** and takes several drugs, so a simple UTI was enough.

steps.text: Anticholinergic drugs cause delirium centrally and **urinary retention** peripherally, which worsens it further.

mcq.q: Over what time course does delirium develop?
mcq.r: Acute onset is the key difference from dementia.

mcq.q: Single most common cause of delirium in the elderly?
Which delirium subtype is most easily missed?
Which drug is a classic anticholinergic cause of delirium?
Standard bedside screening tool for delirium?
mcq.r: Score of 4 or above suggests delirium.

mcq.q: First-line management for all patients with delirium?
Sedation needed in Parkinson's disease: which drug?
Drug used for rapid tranquillisation in delirium?
Which neurotransmitter imbalance is implicated in delirium?
mcq.r: Explains anticholinergic harm and antipsychotic benefit.

points.p: Always search urgently for the cause

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: infection first, then drugs and bowels.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: which one is missed?

points.p: Hypoactive: drowsy and quiet, easily missed

points.why: Agitated at night, drowsy by day.

prompts.q: How does UTI- or drug-related delirium present, and what are the complications?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: peripheral clues point to the cause.

points.p: UTI: agitation, confusion, hallucinations, lower abdominal discomfort

prompts.q: Which features separate delirium from dementia?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: time course and attention.

points.p: Delirium is acute; dementia is gradual

points.why: Lewy body dementia also fluctuates, but over months with parkinsonism.

points.p: Attention is impaired early in delirium

points.p: Score of 4 or above suggests possible delirium

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the common causes decide the tests.

points.p: Stool chart and DRE if constipation suspected

Sedation if needed: low-dose haloperidol, oral then IM

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one fix per trigger.

Anticholinergics precipitate it; antipsychotics can settle it
Cytokines cross the blood-brain barrier in infection

glossary.Delirium: Acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and cognition caused by an underlying illness or drug.
glossary.Dementia: Gradual, progressive decline in memory and thinking over months to years.
glossary.Lewy body dementia: Dementia with fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations and parkinsonism.
glossary.Parkinson's disease: Degenerative dopamine-deficient disorder causing tremor, rigidity and slow movement.
glossary.Hypoactive delirium: Delirium with drowsiness and withdrawal; easily missed.
glossary.Mixed delirium: Delirium alternating between hyperactive and hypoactive features.
glossary.Inattention: Inability to focus or sustain attention; core feature of delirium.
glossary.Fluctuating: Varying over hours, with better and worse periods.
glossary.Disorientation: Not knowing the time, place or person.
glossary.Hallucinations: Seeing or hearing things that are not there.
glossary.Cognitive reserve: The brain's ability to cope with insults before function declines.
glossary.Precipitant: A trigger that brings on a condition.
glossary.4AT: Two-minute bedside delirium screen; a score of 4 or more suggests delirium.
glossary.MMSE: Mini-Mental State Examination, a longer cognitive test used in dementia.
glossary.Anticholinergic: Blocks acetylcholine; causes confusion, dry mouth and urinary retention.
glossary.Promethazine: Sedating antihistamine with strong anticholinergic effects.
glossary.Opioids: Strong painkillers such as morphine and codeine; cause constipation and confusion.
glossary.Urinary retention: Inability to empty the bladder fully.
glossary.Faecal impaction: Hard stool stuck in the rectum, often from opiates and immobility.
glossary.Stool chart: Record of bowel movements, used to spot constipation.
glossary.Re-orientation: Helping a patient know where they are and what time it is, using clocks, calendars and family.
glossary.Verbal de-escalation: Calm, non-confrontational talking to reduce agitation without drugs.
glossary.Haloperidol: Typical antipsychotic (dopamine antagonist) used in low dose for agitated delirium.
glossary.Lorazepam: Benzodiazepine used for sedation when antipsychotics must be avoided, and for rapid tranquillisation.
glossary.Benzodiazepine: Sedative drug class acting on GABA receptors, such as lorazepam.
glossary.Extrapyramidal: Movement side effects of dopamine blockade: stiffness, tremor, slowness.
glossary.Rapid tranquillisation: Urgent use of medication to calm a dangerously agitated patient.
glossary.Cholinergic: Relating to acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter for attention and memory.
glossary.Cytokines: Inflammatory signalling proteins released during infection or surgery.
glossary.Blood-brain barrier: Protective layer controlling what passes from blood into the brain.
glossary.Delirium tremens: Severe alcohol withdrawal with confusion, tremor and hallucinations.
glossary.NICE: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, which publishes UK guidance.
glossary.Donepezil: Cholinesterase inhibitor used in Alzheimer's dementia.

technique.stem: An 82 year old woman is brought in by her son because she has become confused over the last 2 days. She was independent and managing her own finances last week. She is disorientated, cannot follow a conversation and is sleepy one hour and agitated the next. Her temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 136/78 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis of acute confusion in an older patient.

clues: managing her own finances last week
sleepy one hour and agitated the next
steps.x: Acute onset, inattention, fluctuation, possible infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Delirium**, probably infection-driven.

elim: No focal neurology; fluctuating global confusion.
Develops over months; she was well last week.
Does not cause acute inattention and fluctuation.
Months of decline with parkinsonism.

steps.x: **C. Delirium.** Acute + fluctuating + inattention = delirium; find the cause.

technique.stem: A 79 year old man on a surgical ward becomes muddled and drowsy 2 days after a hip replacement. The nurse wants a quick bedside tool to screen for delirium. His temperature is 37.2°C and pulse rate 88 bpm.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate assessment?

steps.x: Screening tool for delirium.
Possible postoperative (hypoactive) delirium.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The **4AT**: 4 or above suggests delirium.

elim: A cognitive test, not a delirium screen.
Not a screening tool; delirium is clinical.
Not used to screen for delirium.
Longer, for dementia assessment.

steps.x: **A. 4AT.** Delirium screen = 4AT.

technique.stem: An 85 year old woman with delirium from a UTI is shouting at staff and trying to leave the ward. She has no history of Parkinson's disease or dementia. One-to-one nursing is in place. Her pulse rate is 94 bpm and BP 148/82 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

steps.x: 'Next step' with risk to others.

clues: shouting at staff and trying to leave
steps.x: Non-drug care in place; now she is a risk.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Verbal de-escalation** first.

elim: Drugs come after de-escalation; oral before IM.
For rapid tranquillisation, not first.
Second-line if de-escalation fails.
Not a first-line step.

steps.x: **E. Verbal de-escalation.** Risk to self or others: de-escalate before sedating.

technique.stem: An 80 year old man is started on promethazine for itch. Two days later he is confused and agitated, with a dry mouth and a palpable bladder.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his delirium?

steps.x: Science: mechanism of a drug-induced delirium.
Anticholinergic drug with peripheral anticholinergic signs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cholinergic deficiency** (with relative dopamine excess).

elim: Dopamine is relatively in excess in delirium.
No headache, vomiting or focal signs.
Serotonin syndrome needs serotonergic drugs and clonus.
Delirium is diffuse dysfunction, not structural.

steps.x: **A. Cholinergic deficiency in the brain.** Anticholinergic drugs cause delirium by deepening the cholinergic deficit.

practice.stem: An 87 year old woman in a care home has become confused and agitated over 24 hours. She has lower abdominal discomfort and is seeing insects on the wall. Staff say she was chatty and orientated 3 days ago. Her temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 130/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Acute confusion with hallucinations, fever and lower abdominal discomfort in an older woman is delirium from a UTI. Dementias develop over months.

steps.x: Diagnosis of acute confusion.
Acute, hallucinations, fever and lower abdominal discomfort: UTI-related delirium.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Delirium**.

elim: Does not cause acute confusion with hallucinations and fever.
Gradual decline over months with parkinsonism.
Gait, incontinence and dementia over months.
Stepwise decline, not 24 hours.

steps.x: **A. Delirium.** Acute change in an older person with infection = delirium.

practice.stem: An 83 year old man is 3 days after a bowel resection. The nurses report he is quiet, withdrawn and sleeping most of the day. When woken he is disorientated and cannot keep his attention on questions. His 4AT score is 7. His pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 124/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A drowsy, quiet patient with inattention and a 4AT of 7 has hypoactive delirium, which is often mistaken for tiredness. Mixed needs alternating agitation.

steps.x: Subtype of delirium.

clues: quiet, withdrawn and sleeping most of the day
steps.x: Acute postoperative inattention; drowsy and quiet.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hypoactive delirium**.

elim: Does not cause acute inattention and disorientation.
He is quiet, not agitated.
Needs alternating agitation; none described.
Gradual or stepwise, not acute after surgery.

steps.x: **C. Hypoactive delirium.** Drowsy, quiet and inattentive = hypoactive delirium; easily missed.

practice.stem: An 81 year old woman was admitted 8 days ago with a vertebral fracture and is on regular oral morphine. Over 2 days she has become confused and restless. She has not opened her bowels for 6 days. Her abdomen is distended. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 138/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her delirium?
practice.e: Constipation from opiates is a common cause of delirium in elderly inpatients. She is afebrile with normal bloods, so infection and metabolic causes are less likely.

steps.x: Cause of delirium.

clues: not opened her bowels for 6 days
steps.x: Inpatient on opiates with no bowel movement.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Constipation** from opiates; check with a DRE.

elim: Calcium is normal.
Glucose is normal.
No focal signs; global fluctuating confusion.
Afebrile with a normal WCC; the bowel history is the clue.

steps.x: **A. Constipation.** Elderly inpatient on opiates + no bowels = constipation.

practice.stem: A 90 year old man in a nursing home has 2 days of new confusion and agitation. Staff note offensive urine and that he is going to the toilet more often. He has had no medication changes. His chest is clear. His temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 128/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his delirium?
practice.e: UTI is the single most common cause of delirium in older people. A clear chest makes pneumonia less likely.

steps.x: Cause of delirium.

clues: going to the toilet more often
steps.x: Fever with urinary symptoms; chest clear.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **UTI**, the single most common cause.

elim: Bowels not mentioned as a problem; urine is the clue.
Glucose is normal.
No new medicines.
Chest is clear.

steps.x: **E. Urinary tract infection.** Infection, especially UTI, is the commonest delirium trigger.

practice.stem: A 78 year old woman was started on a new medicine for allergic itch 3 days ago. She is now confused, with a dry mouth and a palpable bladder. Her other medicines are long-standing. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 140/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which drug is the most likely cause of her delirium?
practice.e: Promethazine is an anticholinergic antihistamine causing delirium, dry mouth and urinary retention. Her other drugs are long-standing and not anticholinergic.

steps.x: Drug cause of delirium.
New antihistamine with central and peripheral anticholinergic effects.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Promethazine**, a sedating anticholinergic antihistamine.

elim: Long-standing and not anticholinergic.
Long-standing; does not cause delirium like this.
Not anticholinergic.
Long-standing; no anticholinergic effect.

steps.x: **D. Promethazine.** New confusion + dry mouth + retention = anticholinergic drug.

practice.stem: A 76 year old man is 2 days after surgery for a hip fracture. At night he is agitated, pulling at his drip and shouting; by day he is drowsy. He drinks 4 units of alcohol a week. Before admission he lived alone and was fully independent. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 146/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Fluctuating agitation and drowsiness after surgery in a previously independent man is delirium. Delirium tremens needs heavy alcohol use and withdrawal.

steps.x: Diagnosis of acute postoperative confusion.
Postoperative, fluctuating, previously well, minimal alcohol.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Delirium** (mixed), triggered by surgery and hospitalisation.

elim: No psychiatric history; fluctuating consciousness points to delirium.
He was independent before; not acute.
He drinks only 4 units a week.
Gradual over months with parkinsonism.

steps.x: **C. Delirium.** New fluctuating confusion after surgery = delirium.

practice.stem: An 86 year old woman has delirium with a 4AT score of 6. She has new urinary frequency and lower abdominal discomfort. Her temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 132/76 mmHg. Her chest is clear and there are no focal neurological signs.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to find the cause?
practice.e: An infection screen including urine culture finds the commonest cause of delirium. Brain imaging is not needed without focal signs or a head injury.

steps.x: Investigation to find the cause of delirium.

clues: urinary frequency and lower abdominal discomfort
steps.x: Delirium with urinary symptoms in an older woman.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urine culture** as part of the infection screen (dipstick unreliable over 65).

elim: No focal signs, fall or anticoagulation.
Not used to find the cause of delirium.
No meningism.
Delirium is from a systemic insult, not structural.

steps.x: **E. Urine culture.** Delirium + urinary symptoms = send a urine culture.

practice.stem: An 84 year old man on regular codeine after a fall has had 3 days of confusion. Nurses have not recorded a bowel movement for 5 days. His abdomen is mildly distended. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
practice.e: A stool chart and DRE are used when constipation or faecal impaction is suspected, especially in elderly inpatients on opiates.

steps.x: Investigation for a suspected cause.

clues: not recorded a bowel movement for 5 days
steps.x: Elderly inpatient on opiates with no bowel movement.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **DRE** (and a stool chart) for faecal impaction.

elim: No focal signs; look for the common cause first.
Not part of the delirium work-up.
No meningism or fever.
No liver disease.

steps.x: **B. Digital rectal examination.** Opiates + no bowels = DRE.

practice.stem: A 79 year old woman has delirium from a chest infection. She is calm but disorientated and keeps asking where she is. She is not a risk to herself or others. Her pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 128/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management of her delirium?
practice.e: One-to-one supervision and reorientation (clocks, calendars, family, lighting, hydration) is first-line for all patients with delirium. Drugs are only for risk.

steps.x: Initial management of delirium.

clues: not a risk to herself or others
steps.x: Delirium without risk.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **One-to-one supervision and reorientation**.

elim: For rapid tranquillisation; she is calm.
A dementia drug, not delirium treatment.
Only if sedation is needed; she is calm.
Never first-line.

steps.x: **B. One-to-one supervision and reorientation.** Delirium first-line = non-drug care for everyone.

practice.stem: A 77 year old man with Parkinson's disease has delirium from a UTI. Despite one-to-one care and verbal de-escalation he is hitting staff and trying to climb out of bed. His pulse rate is 100 bpm and BP 150/86 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate medication?
practice.e: In Parkinson's disease or Lewy body dementia, antipsychotics worsen extrapyramidal symptoms, so a benzodiazepine such as oral lorazepam is used.

steps.x: Medication choice in a special group: Parkinson's.

clues: Despite one-to-one care and verbal de-escalation
steps.x: Sedation needed in Parkinson's.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A **benzodiazepine**: oral lorazepam.

elim: Antipsychotics worsen Parkinson's (extrapyramidal effects).
Anticholinergic; worsens delirium.
Avoid antipsychotics in Parkinson's.
Still an antipsychotic; avoid.

steps.x: **D. Oral lorazepam.** Parkinson's or Lewy body + sedation = lorazepam, never an antipsychotic.

practice.stem: An 83 year old woman has delirium from pneumonia. One-to-one care and verbal de-escalation have failed and she keeps trying to climb over the bed rails. She has no history of Parkinson's disease or Lewy body dementia. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 138/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
practice.e: If sedation is needed and the patient does not have Parkinson's or Lewy body dementia, low-dose haloperidol is second-line. Anticholinergics worsen delirium.

steps.x: 'Next step' after non-drug measures fail.

clues: no history of Parkinson's disease or Lewy body dementia
steps.x: Needs sedation; antipsychotics are allowed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Low-dose haloperidol**, oral before IM.

elim: A dementia drug; does not settle acute agitation.
Anticholinergic; makes delirium worse.
Not appropriate as the next step.
Anticholinergic antihistamine; worsens delirium.

steps.x: **B. Low-dose haloperidol.** No Parkinson's or Lewy body = haloperidol second-line.

practice.stem: A 74 year old man develops acute confusion and inattention on day 2 of severe pneumonia. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg. CT head is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his delirium?
practice.e: Inflammatory cytokines from infection cross the blood-brain barrier and disrupt neuronal function. Delirium is diffuse dysfunction, not structural brain disease.

steps.x: Science: why infection causes delirium.
Systemic infection with a normal brain scan.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Inflammatory **cytokines** cross the blood-brain barrier and disrupt neurons.

elim: That would be meningitis or encephalitis; he has no meningism.
Not stated; the mechanism is inflammatory.
CT is normal.
Delirium is diffuse dysfunction, not structural damage.

steps.x: **B. Cytokines crossing the blood-brain barrier.** Infection delirium = cytokines across the BBB.
